Where am I going today if I'm going anywhere at all without my soul, that bird with its unreadable, unheard name having wandered off again, convinced that it is more than just a word— do we travel far from each other today?— me in my pre-owned Mazda with my radio full of wasps' nest news, my Peshawar & my Rupert Murdoch, all my guilty Murdochs— my destination like a homestead made of fallen maple leaves, the three leaves that form a tipi tipped together by a 5-year-old's hands, a dwelling place, where if I wanted to I could rest my human rights while my soul travels far from its base, lost for a while on its own highly privatized trip, the idea of living forever an idea that is not an eternity at all for my wanderer but a wish the bird has to fly brocaded by herself within the borders of a tapestry, far from some witch queen's cackle, far from that witch who has disguised herself as a sparhawk woven out of dark thread by a Flemish peasant's hands— how far is too far, you ask?— a little foolishness goes a long, long way, I'd say; a lot drops dead in its tracks.

outputs.L1: Where am I bound today—if indeed I am bound anywhere at all—without my soul, that bird bearing its unreadable, unheard name, having wandered off once more, convinced that it is something more than a mere word? Do we travel far from one another today?—I in my pre-owned Mazda, its radio abuzz with a hornet's nest of news, my Peshawar and my Rupert Murdoch, all my guilty Murdochs—my destination like a homestead fashioned from fallen maple leaves, three of them arranged into a tipi by a five-year-old's hands, a dwelling place where, should I so wish, I might lay down my human rights while my soul journeys far from its home, lost for a time upon its own most privatized excursion. The notion of living forever is, for my wanderer, no eternity at all, but rather the bird's yearning to fly, embroidered by her own hand within the borders of a tapestry, far from some witch queen's cackle, far from that witch who has disguised herself as a sparhawk, spun from dark thread by a Flemish peasant's hands. How far is too far, you ask? A little foolishness, I would say, goes a long, long way; a great deal drops dead in its tracks.
outputs.L2: Where do I head today, if I'm heading anywhere at all, stripped of my soul—that bird whose name can't be read or spoken, which has drifted off yet again, certain it amounts to something greater than a mere word—will the two of us drift a great distance apart today? Here I sit in my secondhand Mazda, the radio buzzing with news like an angry hive, broadcasting Peshawar and Rupert Murdoch, every one of my shameful Murdochs. My endpoint resembles a little house built from fallen maple leaves—three of them arranged into a tipi, propped together by the fingers of a child of five, a small shelter where, should I choose, I might lay down my human rights while my soul journeys far from where it began, briefly gone on its own thoroughly privatized excursion. The notion of living without end is, for my wandering bird, no eternity whatsoever but simply a longing—the desire to soar embroidered by her own self inside the edges of a tapestry, distant from the shrieking laughter of some witch queen, distant from that witch who has taken the shape of a sparhawk, spun from dark thread by the hands of a peasant from Flanders. And how far, you might ask, is too far? A small measure of folly, I'd answer, carries you an enormous distance; a great deal of it collapses lifeless on the spot.

# Reflections on a Wandering Soul

There are moments when I feel utterly disconnected from my own soul, as though it has slipped away from me entirely. I imagine it as a nameless bird, one that has quietly taken flight and wandered off on some separate journey of its own—a path I cannot follow or even name.

The strangeness of this feeling deepens against the backdrop of ordinary life. Here I am, driving my used Mazda through familiar streets, the radio filling the air with troubling news—the tragedy of Peshawar, the manipulations of Murdoch media. The mundane machinery of my daily existence stands in stark contrast to wherever my soul now travels in its quiet, spiritual wandering. The gap between these two realities feels almost absurd.

In my imagination, I construct a refuge for that soul: a fragile shelter built from maple leaves, delicate and childlike. It is a place where all the weight of human concerns—our endless debates about rights, our arguments and anxieties—could be gently set aside. A place simply to rest, without demand or expectation.

I have come to understand the soul's longing for immortality differently than I once did. It is not, I think, a grand desire for eternity at all. Rather, it is something far more modest and tender: the simple wish to fly freely, like a bird woven into an ancient tapestry, forever escaping the threatening figure of the witch who pursues it. It asks not for endless time, but only for the freedom of flight.

And so I arrive at a final reflection, one about limits and excess. Perhaps a small measure of foolishness is what allows us to endure—a little unreason that keeps us alive and moving. But too much of it, like anything taken to excess, leads only to ruin.

# Spiritual Dislocation in Motion: A Reading

The poem opens onto a deceptively mundane scene—a person behind the wheel, engaged in the most routine of activities. Yet within this ordinary drive, something extraordinary unravels. The speaker experiences a profound sense of spiritual dislocation, as though the very act of movement through physical space triggers a corresponding fracture in the psyche. The self, that everyday operator of the vehicle, becomes suddenly aware of its separation from the soul, and this recognition transforms the commute into a meditation on estrangement.

Central to the poem's surreal architecture is the image of a wandering bird-soul. The soul, no longer anchored to the body, takes flight—an untethered creature drifting away from the speaker who remains fixed in the driver's seat. This avian metaphor captures the paradox of the modern condition: even as the body is transported swiftly and efficiently toward its destination, the soul may wander in an entirely different direction, or lag behind, or lose itself altogether. The bird becomes an emblem of that part of the self which cannot be steered or controlled, which follows its own migratory logic.

Surrounding this inner drama is the noise of media-saturated modernity. The poem gestures toward a world thick with signals, broadcasts, and information—the ambient static of contemporary life that fills every silence and colonizes every moment of stillness. This saturation contributes to the speaker's disconnection; the more the external world clamors for attention, the more distant the soul becomes. Modernity, in this reading, is not a bridge to connection but a source of it profound alienation, drowning out the quieter registers of interior life.

The image of a woven tapestry offers another lens through which the poem interrogates distance and disconnection. A tapestry is at once a unified whole and an assembly of countless individual threads. It suggests the interconnectedness of experience, but also its constructed, artificial quality—the way meaning is stitched together rather than found. The speaker seems to examine the tapestry of their own existence, tracing the threads that bind self to soul, past to present, and finding those threads stretched thin, frayed, or pulled to breaking across unbridgeable gaps.

Threading through the entire piece is the persistent question: "how far is too far?" This refrain gives the poem its philosophical spine. How far can the soul wander before it cannot return? How far can the self travel from its own center before the journey becomes irreversible? The question is asked without expectation of a definitive answer, and this open-endedness is precisely the point. Distance, the poem suggests, resists measurement when it is spiritual rather than merely spatial.

The poem's wry conclusion offers its most memorable insight: foolishness, unlike wisdom or life itself, travels endlessly. Where wisdom might know when to stop and where life inevitably reaches its terminus in death, foolishness knows no such limits. It goes on and on, unbounded, immortal in its own absurd way. This observation carries a dark comedy, for it inverts our usual hierarchies—we prize wisdom and cling to life, yet it is our folly that proves most durable and far-reaching.

In this final turn, the poem delivers a meditation on mortality, meaning, and the elusive nature of the self. Life is finite; the drive will end; the body will eventually cease its motion. Wisdom, too, has its limits, arriving late and departing early. But the self remains fundamentally elusive—as ungraspable as a bird in flight, as intricate and dispersed as threads in a tapestry. What endures, the poem suggests with a rueful smile, is not our best qualities but our capacity for foolishness, which travels farther than we ever intended to go.

If you are wondering **where** to buy or rent a **Mazda** in **Peshawar**, you have several practical options to explore in this bustling city of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In Pakistan, the term "Mazda" is commonly used to describe medium-sized trucks and transport vehicles, which are widely used for moving goods and passengers across the region.

- **GT Road Dealerships** – Several dealers along the Grand Trunk Road offer transport vehicles suitable for business use.
- **Local Transport Stands** – For those looking to hire a Mazda for cargo or moving purposes, transport stands throughout the city connect customers with drivers and vehicle owners.

## Why Mazda Vehicles Are Popular Here

In Peshawar, Mazda trucks are valued for their durability and reliability, making them ideal for transporting goods to nearby areas, tribal districts, and even across the border for trade. Many small business owners rely on these vehicles for daily commercial activities.

2. Inspect the vehicle's condition and documentation.
3. Verify registration and ownership papers.
4. Take a test drive to assess performance.

With careful research, finding the right Mazda vehicle in Peshawar can be a smooth and rewarding experience.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem about a morning commute in which the speaker imagines their soul wandering off as a bird with an unpronounceable name, weaving in images of news radio, a used car, and a medieval tapestry.
counterfactuals.output:
# Migration

And so the ignition turns and something in me lifts—the traffic light bleeds green and I am pulling out, but no, some part of me is *pulling up*, feathering skyward while the rest stays buckled to the driver's seat of this used Corolla, this hundred-and-forty-thousand-mile confessional, this box that still smells faintly of the previous owner's cigarettes and someone else's rosary swinging from the mirror like a small forgotten prayer—

the radio says *and in other news* and *the death toll* and *meanwhile officials warn* and I am nodding at the windshield like I understand, like understanding is a thing you do at seven a.m. with cold coffee sweating in the cupholder, and somewhere above the overpass my soul has become a bird whose name I cannot say, a name with too many consonants and a diphthong that would split my tongue, a bird stitched from vowels I've never learned—

*and gas prices*, the radio insists, *and the mayor responded*—

but the bird, the bird is banking now over the strip malls and the median grass, and I think of that tapestry I saw once behind glass, the one where the unicorn kneels bewildered in its little fenced garden, all those thousands of hands over all those hundreds of years pulling thread through warp to make a single red pomegranate, a single tame astonishment, and how the whole thing was *someone's morning*, was labor, was the medieval version of merging left—

and *traffic on the fives*, says the voice, *and expect delays*—

and my soul the bird with the unpronounceable name does not care about delays, does not carry the toll or the death or the response, only rides the thermal off the asphalt, only knows the direction *away*, and I want to follow but the light is green again and the man behind me leans on his horn like it owes him something, and I press the pedal, I rejoin the herd of taillights, I come back down into the used and rattling body of my day—

*and now, the weather*—

and the bird gets smaller, a loose thread, a stitch coming out of the sky's blue cloth, and I mouth its name I cannot say, I mouth it anyway, all breath and no sound, and I drive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem that blends the mundane (a pre-owned Mazda, radio news about Peshawar and Rupert Murdoch) with the surreal and mythic (a soul-bird, a witch queen disguised as a sparhawk woven by a Flemish peasant), ending on a wry aphorism about foolishness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Odometer, Reading the Weather of Souls**

The Mazda came to me pre-owned, which is to say
someone else's grief had already worn grooves
into the driver's seat, a lumbar cursive
I learned to read at every red light.

               Peshawar, says the radio,
               and then a pause the size of a country,
                              and then: *Rupert Murdoch*,
as if the two were weather fronts colliding
somewhere above the dashboard's cracked meridian.

I merged. The soul-bird rode shotgun,
small brown nothing with a chest of ash,
pecking at the check-engine light
as though it were a seed of wisdom
God had planted in the console.

               (You should know:
               the witch queen travels now
               disguised as a sparhawk
               woven by a Flemish peasant
               into a tapestry that hangs
               in a museum gift shop
               reproduced on a tea towel
               you can purchase for €12.)

She looks down from the linen
with the patience of the thoroughly damned,
and the soul-bird recognizes her,
and does not flinch,
because a soul-bird has seen this trick before—

               the empire folded into a peasant's loom,
               Peshawar folded into the news,
               the news folded into the little cloth
               that wipes the wineglass clean.

Murdoch, the radio insists.
The sparhawk does not blink.
The Mazda idles like an animal
that has forgotten it was ever wild.

And I drive on, carrying my ash-chested passenger,
past the off-ramp, past the tapestry, past the burning,

               having learned the one thing
               every pre-owned vehicle teaches its second fool:

*that we are always paying off
the debts of a man we never met,
and calling it, quite proudly, ownership.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long, single-sentence poem in the voice of someone questioning where they and their soul are traveling, mixing contemporary references with fairy-tale imagery of birds, tapestries, and witches.
counterfactuals.output:
Where am I going, and is my soul packed in the carry-on beside me,

buckled into seat 23C with its phone at four percent and no charger,

as we taxi past the gate where a woman in a green apron pours oat milk

into paper cups that dissolve like the breadcrumb trails we were promised

would lead us home, though the birds—those glossy, GPS-eyed starlings—

ate the map before I could screenshot it, before I could tag the constellation

my grandmother stitched into a tapestry now folded in a storage unit

off the interstate, gathering the dust of every unanswered text,

and I keep asking the flight attendant, the barista, the algorithm

that knows my heart rate and my three a.m. searches, whether the witch

in the terminal news—the one who sells us mirrors that only show

our best angle, who cackles softly through the speakers announcing delays—

is the same witch from the woods, or just her granddaughter in a blazer,

and whether the spindle I pricked my thumb on was a needle or a notification,

and where, oh where, does the soul deplane, in what fluorescent baggage claim

does it circle the carousel forever, one unclaimed thing among the black bags,

waiting for a hand it half-remembers, waiting for the thread to pull it back

through the loom, the fog, the boarding groups, the woods, the glowing exit signs,

toward some warm lit window I can't yet name but ache to be arriving at?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary lyric poem that meditates on the separation of body and soul during a car ride, using childhood imagery like maple leaves forming a tipi, and closing with a folksy saying about foolishness.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Knows on the Interstate

The soul goes ahead of me
by half a second, always—
it has already arrived
where my hands still grip the wheel,
still steer through the ordinary dusk.

I am two people at seventy miles an hour:
one who drives,
one who remembers
being small enough to believe
that maple leaves could be gathered,

their five-fingered hands
leaned together like poles,
a tipi the size of my sitting-down,
red and gold and secretly rotting,
a house I could almost enter

if I were only smaller,
if the body could fold
the way paper folds,
the way light folds
into the corner of a moving window.

Now the mile markers pass
like the years pass—
I am here and not here,
the flesh keeping its patient appointment
with arrival,

the spirit gone loose in the trees
along the shoulder,
crouched again in that leaf-house
that never held anyone,
that collapsed the moment I let go.

My grandmother used to say:
*Only a fool tries to carry water
in a basket—
but the basket comes home wet,
and isn't that something to have held.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a densely allusive, digressive poem about mortality and the desire to live forever, framed as a monologue during a drive, incorporating pop-culture and political references alongside images of a bird trapped in a woven tapestry.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Commute Toward Never

Drive, then. The dashboard glows its little green apocalypse,
and I am telling you, again, about the bird—
you weren't listening, you were checking whether the world
had ended on your phone, which it hadn't, quite,
just the usual: a president somewhere gesturing
at a crowd like a conductor of a symphony of ash,
and the ticker running its low fever underneath.

But the bird. In the tapestry my grandmother left,
a heron woven mid-flight into the millefleurs,
and here's the thing that keeps me up—it can't complete the arc.
Forever rising, forever stitched to rising,
its wing a permanent hypothesis. I envy it.
I do. To be caught in the loom's amber and never
to arrive at the hard shoulder where the arriving ends.

Signal left. The Nissan behind us has a bumper sticker
about the rapture, which is optimism, honestly,
a scheduled exit, an assumption, a first-class seat.
I want that certainty the way I wanted, once,
to be Bowie—not the songs, the shedding,
the serial resurrection, Ziggy into Thin White
into the man who died on schedule anyway,
having rehearsed it in the video, *look up here, I'm in heaven*.

Even he. Even the ones who curated their own ghosts.
Even Ozymandias with his good publicist.
The two vast trunkless legs, the sneer of cold command
now cropped and captioned, scrolling, *mood.*
We laugh because the alternative is merges-ahead,
is the odometer that only ever counts one way.

You ask if I'm okay. The exit signs go by
like flashcards for a test I'm failing gently.
I'm thinking of the pharaohs and their canopic jars,
the organs sorted lovingly for a next life
that was, let's be honest, a start-up that never shipped.
I'm thinking of Elon promising to back us up to Mars,
the cloud, the blockchain, the cold storage of the soul—
new gods, same jar, we sort ourselves and hope.

The heron. Threads don't age. That's the trick of it.
The wool remembers nothing, wants for nothing,
holds the whole warm-blooded panic of a flight
without the flight, without the falling that flight implies.
I press the pedal. Sixty. Sixty-five.
There is no speed that outruns the destination,
which is the joke Achilles never got
chasing that tortoise down the interstate of Zeno's grief.

And politics—god, the *forever* they all promise,
the term limits repealed, the strongman in his bronze,
the constitution amended toward a single endless *now*—
it's the same hunger, isn't it, just wearing a flag.
The wish to woven-in, to millefleurs, to never
reach the border of ourselves and show our documents.

We're almost there. The sky does that dissolving thing.
I'll park. We'll go inside. We'll be, for one more evening,
unfinished, which is only the polite word for alive.
But leave the engine running a moment. Let me watch
the little green apocalypse a while longer,
the heron on the seat-back of my mind still rising,
still not arrived, still ours, still not, still—

merge.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
